sentences.text: This dinosaur grew to lengths of 5 to 5.5 meters and weighed between 1.8 and 2.7 metric tons.
It stood approximately 1.8 meters tall at the hips.
Its mouth featured a beak and shearing cheek teeth arranged in continuous dental batteries for slicing plants.
The animal possessed a relatively short tail.
Lawrence Lambe named the species in 1913 after Charles H. Sternberg found the first skull on the southwest bank of the Red Deer River in the summer of that year.
Lambe described this initial find as the holotype, which is the specific specimen the species is based on.
Evidence from bone beds suggests the animal likely lived in large herds.
Several species previously assigned to this genus have been reassigned to other genera, including the proposal of Rubeosaurus as a synonym.

The species S. parksi is now accepted as a specimen of S. albertensis, while S. sphenocerus was originally described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1890 as a species of Monoclonius before being attributed to Styracosaurus in 1915.
Fossils date to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous and were found in the Dinosaur Park Formation near Steveville, Alberta.

The function of the horns and frills has been debated for many years. The classification of S. ovatus is also debated, having been moved to Rubeosaurus in 2010 but potentially returned to Styracosaurus or considered a separate genus again since 2020. Robert Holmes and colleagues considered S. ovatus to be a junior synonym of S. albertensis, whereas John Wilson and colleagues advised retaining it as a separate species, possibly directly descended from S. albertensis. It has been suggested that S. albertensis evolved directly from Centrosaurus and subsequently into the later species Rubeosaurus ovatus.
